title: Subcutaneous Amivantamab plus Pembrolizumab in Recurrent/Metastatic HNSCC (OrigAMI-4, OrigAMI-5)
breakthrough: Amivantamab, an EGFR-MET bispecific antibody, has a head and neck programme. In cohort 2 of the phase 1b/2 OrigAMI-4 study, 39 patients with previously untreated PD-L1-positive, HPV-unrelated recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma received subcutaneous amivantamab plus pembrolizumab every three weeks and achieved a confirmed objective response rate of 56% (95% CI 40 to 72) with the expected safety profile. Subcutaneous amivantamab has Breakthrough Therapy Designation in HNSCC, and the global phase 3 OrigAMI-5 is randomising about 500 first-line HPV-unrelated patients to amivantamab plus pembrolizumab and carboplatin versus pembrolizumab plus platinum chemotherapy with or without 5-fluorouracil.
impact: Adds a targeted antibody to first-line immunotherapy in the HPV-unrelated phenotype, which is the group with the worst outcomes and the least benefit from HPV-era de-escalation.
practical: The setting is first-line recurrent or metastatic disease, not downstaging before salvage surgery — the two are different conversations and the trial data only support the former. Read the response rate against its denominator: 39 patients in a single-arm phase 1b/2 cohort, with phase 3 not yet reported. Subcutaneous administration matters practically, reducing infusion time and infusion-related reactions.
link: OrigAMI-4 — amivantamab plus pembrolizumab in previously untreated recurrent/metastatic HNSCC

verify.status: matched with corrections — the drug does have a real HNSCC programme
verify.note: VERIFIED, AND A PREVIOUS SUSPICION OF MINE WAS WRONG. Amivantamab appeared as a wrong-drug title twice earlier in this review — substituted for anti-amyloid antibodies in neurology and for an ocular surface agent in ophthalmology — and I flagged this ENT entry as probably the third instance. It is not. There is a genuine HNSCC programme: OrigAMI-4 cohort 2 (39 patients, first-line PD-L1-positive HPV-unrelated R/M HNSCC, subcutaneous amivantamab plus pembrolizumab, confirmed ORR 56%), Breakthrough Therapy Designation for subcutaneous amivantamab in HNSCC, and the phase 3 OrigAMI-5 enrolling ~500 patients. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) The submission's practical claim — a regimen 'to shrink locally advanced or recurrent tumors prior to re-resection or palliative care' — is not the tested setting; this is first-line recurrent/metastatic treatment, not neoadjuvant downstaging. (2) 'Clinical trials demonstrated high efficacy' is sized: one single-arm cohort of 39, phase 3 unreported. Also named the mechanism (EGFR-MET bispecific), which the submission omits and which is the reason the drug is being tried here at all.

title: OTOF Gene Therapy: Durability to 2.5 Years and an Expanding Age Range
breakthrough: Follow-up of AAV-OTOF gene therapy for autosomal recessive deafness 9 now extends to 2.5 years in a multicentre report, showing that restored hearing persists rather than fading. A separate cohort of ten patients followed for 6 to 12 months included a teenager and a young adult, extending treatment beyond the infants and young children of the first trials. Auditory brainstem responses and speech acquisition have been maintained in the bilaterally treated children.
impact: Durability was the open question after the first-in-human results, and the answer so far is that the effect holds. The age-range expansion matters more than it appears: it suggests the therapeutic window is not confined to the first years of life in this specific genetic form of deafness.
practical: The consequence for practice is that genomic sequencing has to be available early enough to identify candidates, and that an older child or young adult with OTOF deafness should not be assumed to have missed the window. Keep the scope in view — the follow-up is 2.5 years, not a lifetime; the cohorts are small and single-arm; and this applies to OTOF-related deafness, which is a minority of congenital hearing loss.
link: Nature — multicentre gene therapy for OTOF-related deafness followed up to 2.5 years

verify.status: corrected — title contained an orthopaedic term, and the pathway claim is premature
verify.note: The underlying results are real: multicentre OTOF gene therapy follow-up to 2.5 years published in Nature, and a ten-patient cohort with 6-12 months of follow-up that included a teenager and a young adult. THREE CORRECTIONS. (1) TITLE: submitted as 'Microfracture & Gene Therapy Scaling for Congenital Sensorineural Hearing Loss'. Microfracture is an orthopaedic cartilage technique with no meaning in otology — a wrong-term title of the same class as the wrong-drug titles found in neurology and ophthalmology, and it survives a skim because the body text is about gene therapy. Removed. (2) 'Formally establishes targeted gene delivery into the infant scala media as a standard therapeutic pathway alongside early cochlear implantation' overstates it — no guideline establishes this as standard, and the entry now says durability and age range are what the data show. (3) 'Pediatric otologists now routinely integrate comprehensive genomic sequencing during newborn screening' is aspirational rather than current practice; reworded as what needs to happen for candidates to be found. DEDUPLICATION NOTE: the 2025 list carries the first-in-human restoration result. This entry is kept as a separate development because durability past two years and the age-range extension are new findings rather than a restatement, and the two entries have been written so they do not overlap.

title: Hyperangulated versus Macintosh-Geometry Videolaryngoscopy in the Difficult Airway
breakthrough: A randomised controlled trial in adults with an anticipated difficult airway found hyperangulated videolaryngoscopy gave a better glottic view, higher first-attempt success, greater success with the first-line technique and shorter intubation times than Macintosh-geometry videolaryngoscopy. The trade-off is consistent across the literature: a hyperangulated blade sees around the corner but makes advancing the tube harder, and first-attempt success falls and intubation time rises when the tube introducer is not matched to the blade.
impact: Shifts blade selection from operator habit toward anticipated anatomy, and makes the introducer part of the decision rather than an afterthought.
practical: For an anticipated anterior or difficult glottis, reach for the hyperangulated blade — and have the matched rigid stylet or channelled tube ready, because the view is not the hard part. For a routine airway a standard-geometry blade remains reasonable. Note that the evidence base sits in anaesthesia and emergency airway practice rather than in head and neck surgery, and that several frequently cited comparisons are manikin or cadaver studies rather than patient trials.
link: Anaesthesia — hyperangulated versus Macintosh videolaryngoscopy in anticipated difficult airway management

verify.status: NOT FOUND as cited — real evidence substituted
verify.note: The specific citation does not check out. The submission names 'The ANGLE Trial' with registration NCT07223762 and calls it multi-centre randomised controlled trial data providing 'definitive guidance'. No trial of that name or registration number surfaced, and the NCT number should not be repeated. Real evidence on the same question does exist and has been substituted: Köhl et al. in Anaesthesia (2024), a randomised controlled trial in anticipated difficult airways favouring hyperangulated videolaryngoscopy on glottic view, first-attempt success and intubation time; a 2025 randomised trial of Glidescope versus an intermediate-angled blade; and a registered systematic review protocol. The tube-advancement trade-off has been added because it is the reason the answer is not simply 'use hyperangulated'. Also flagged that this is substantively an airway-management topic drawn from anaesthesia and emergency medicine rather than an ENT trial, and that several commonly quoted comparisons are manikin or cadaver studies — the submission's 'definitive' is not warranted by any of them.

title: Endoscopic Sinus Surgery and Biologics in Chronic Rhinosinusitis: No Head-to-Head Trial Yet
breakthrough: There is still no randomised trial comparing functional endoscopic sinus surgery directly against biologic therapy. What exists is indirect: a network meta-analysis of five randomised trials and 1,748 patients set endoscopic sinus surgery with medical therapy alongside dupilumab, benralizumab, mepolizumab and omalizumab in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, and a separate multicentre randomised trial established that sinus surgery plus medical therapy beats medical therapy alone on symptoms, quality of life and systemic corticosteroid use. Sequencing — which to do first, and when — is being addressed in review rather than in trials.
impact: The clinically important fact is the absence. Decisions about surgery versus a biologic costing tens of thousands of dollars a year are being made on indirect comparison, and the field knows it.
practical: Surgery first remains defensible in the polyp patient with obstructing disease, osteitis or fungal disease, since the randomised evidence for surgery against medical therapy alone is solid and the operation is a one-off. A biologic is the option for the patient who has had adequate surgery and continues to recur. Be explicit with patients that the sequence has not been settled by a trial, and treat any claim of 'precise phenotypic markers' indicating one over the other with scepticism.
link: Network meta-analysis — comparative short-term efficacy of endoscopic sinus surgery and biologics in CRSwNP

verify.status: NOT FOUND as described — the head-to-head trial does not exist
verify.note: The submission describes 'Phase III randomized trial data published in JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery' comparing FESS against ongoing biologic therapy in recurrent acute and non-polypoid chronic rhinosinusitis, and says it 'updates care pathways to define precise phenotypic markers' for choosing between them. No such trial was found. What exists is a network meta-analysis (five RCTs, 1,748 patients, indirect comparison of ESS plus medical therapy against four monoclonals in CRSwNP), a multicentre RCT of ESS plus medical therapy versus medical therapy alone, and narrative work on timing. Rewritten so the entry's content is the absence of a head-to-head trial, which is genuinely useful to know and is the honest answer to the question the submission was asking. Note also that the submission specifies the NON-polypoid phenotype, where the 2025 AAO-HNS guideline recommends against routine biologics anyway — so a trial pitting surgery against biologics in that group would be testing something already advised against.

title: Circulating Tumour HPV DNA for Post-Treatment Surveillance in Oropharyngeal Cancer
journal: Clinical Cancer Research and multi-site clinical series
breakthrough: Assays for circulating tumour tissue-modified viral HPV DNA are now validated for surveillance after treatment of HPV-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma. In prospective surveillance, patients with undetectable ctHPVDNA at every post-treatment time point had a 100% negative predictive value, while two consecutively positive tests carried a 94% positive predictive value for recurrence, with a median lead time of 3.9 months before biopsy-proven recurrence. A retrospective series of 1,076 patients across 108 US sites found the assay positive in 7.4%, with a 95% positive predictive value, and it was commonly the first indication of recurrence in asymptomatic patients.
impact: Gives head and neck surveillance a blood test with a genuinely useful negative predictive value, in a disease where examination and imaging of a treated neck are both difficult to interpret.
practical: Act on two consecutive positives, not one — the single-test positive predictive value does not support committing a patient to further imaging or biopsy, and the published figures are built on consecutive testing. A negative result is strong reassurance. Note the assay design: it is a targeted tissue-modified viral HPV DNA test, not whole-genome sequencing, and it only applies to HPV-associated disease, so it does nothing for the HPV-unrelated patient.
link: Clinical Cancer Research — detection of occult recurrence using circulating tumour tissue-modified viral HPV DNA

verify.status: matched with corrections — supported, one technical description wrong
verify.note: Verified and strongly supported: 100% negative predictive value with consistently undetectable ctHPVDNA, 94% positive predictive value on two consecutive positives, median 3.9-month lead time before biopsy-proven recurrence, and a 1,076-patient series across 108 sites with 95% positive predictive value where the biomarker was often the first sign of recurrence in asymptomatic patients. Those figures have been added — the submission asserted the capability without any. ONE CORRECTION: the submission calls it 'liquid biopsy whole-genome sequencing assays'. It is a targeted tissue-modified viral HPV DNA assay, not whole-genome sequencing, and describing it wrongly would mislead a resident about cost, turnaround and what the test can detect. Also added that the two-consecutive-positive rule is what the predictive values rest on, and that the test is useless in HPV-unrelated disease — the submission's 'first-line postoperative surveillance tool' reads as though it applies to all oropharyngeal cancer.

title: Intralesional PD-1 Blockade for Oral Epithelial Dysplasia
breakthrough: A first-in-human dose-escalation trial injected nivolumab directly into oral epithelial dysplasia — 10 mg or 20 mg, roughly 2 to 4% of the intravenous dose — every three weeks for four cycles in 29 patients, 15 with high-grade and 14 with low-grade dysplasia, over half of the lesions on the tongue. At a median follow-up of 14.5 months, 25 of 29 (85%) had a clinical response with lesion area falling by an average of 60%, 12 (41%) showed histological downgrading, and 6 had a complete pathological response with no dysplasia remaining. Quality of life was preserved. A randomised placebo-controlled phase 2 is enrolling at MD Anderson (NCT06561087).
impact: Opens the possibility of treating an oral precancer pharmacologically instead of resecting or ablating it, at a fraction of the systemic dose and therefore a fraction of the immune-related toxicity.
practical: Not yet an alternative to surgery outside a trial — the phase 2 is what will establish whether it prevents progression to carcinoma, which is the outcome that matters and which a phase 1 cannot answer. Its natural candidate is the patient with widespread leukoplakia or erythroplakia in whom resection would cost speech or swallowing. The same approach is being extended to cervical, anal and cutaneous dysplasia.
link: The ASCO Post — intralesional PD-1 blockade promising for oral cancer prevention

verify.status: matched with corrections — real, and stronger than submitted
verify.note: Verified. A first-in-human intralesional nivolumab trial in oral epithelial dysplasia was presented at AACR 2026, with results better than the submission conveys: 29 patients, 85% clinical response, mean 60% reduction in lesion area, 41% histological downgrading, 6 complete pathological responses, median follow-up 14.5 months, quality of life preserved, and a randomised placebo-controlled phase 2 now enrolling (NCT06561087). All of that has been added. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) Phase: submitted as 'Phase I/II trials'; this is a single first-in-human phase 1 dose-escalation study. (2) The submission says it 'introduces a organ-preserving therapeutic alternative to broad surgical mucosal resection or laser ablation'. A phase 1 does not establish an alternative to surgery — progression to carcinoma was not the endpoint — so the entry states that the phase 2 is what will answer it. Related background: a JAMA Oncology non-randomised trial of systemic nivolumab in high-risk oral leukoplakia preceded this work.

title: Proton Beam Therapy versus IMRT for Oropharyngeal Cancer (TORPEdO)
breakthrough: TORPEdO is a phase 3 randomised trial of intensity-modulated proton therapy against IMRT in oropharyngeal cancer, and it delivers level I evidence on toxicity. Grade 3 acute events were less frequent with protons: mucositis 37% versus 54%, dysphagia 12% versus 24%, the mucositis difference tracking a lower planned median oral cavity dose (36.5 Gy versus 47.2 Gy). Moderate-to-severe xerostomia was lower late as well — 6% versus 20% at 18 to 24 months (P = 0.025) and 6% versus 20% at 24 to 36 months (P = 0.01).
impact: Converts the dosimetric argument for protons into measured patient outcomes. Sparing the oral cavity and salivary glands produces less mucositis acutely and less dry mouth years later, which is the difference between surviving the treatment and living well after it.
practical: Route candidates toward proton therapy where access and funding allow, and use these figures in the discussion: roughly a threefold difference in moderate-to-severe xerostomia at two to three years is what the patient will actually notice. Be careful with oncologic claims — TORPEdO's demonstrated result is toxicity reduction; survival and disease control are reported separately and the trial was not designed as an oncologic non-inferiority study.
link: The Lancet — proton beam therapy for oropharyngeal cancer (TORPEdO): a phase 3, randomised controlled trial

verify.status: matched with corrections — supported, with the oncologic claim qualified
verify.note: Verified and well supported. TORPEdO is a real phase 3 randomised trial published in The Lancet in 2026, and the direction the submission gives — equivalent control with less xerostomia and dysphagia — matches the toxicity findings. Numbers added: grade 3 acute mucositis 37% versus 54%, dysphagia 12% versus 24%, planned median oral cavity dose 36.5 versus 47.2 Gy, moderate-to-severe xerostomia 6% versus 20% at both 18-24 and 24-36 months. ONE CORRECTION: the submission leads with 'demonstrates equivalent oncologic control'. TORPEdO's demonstrated result is toxicity; survival and disease-control outcomes are reported in a companion paper and the trial was not powered as an oncologic non-inferiority study, so equivalence should not be asserted from it. Reworded, with the toxicity numbers carrying the entry.

title: Laryngopharyngeal Reflux: Diet, Alginates and Restraint with PPIs
date: 2017, with a subsequent alginate randomised trial
breakthrough: A comparison of alkaline water plus a 90 to 95% whole-food, plant-based Mediterranean-style diet plus standard reflux precautions against proton pump inhibition plus the same precautions found the dietary approach at least as effective for laryngopharyngeal reflux: 62.6% of dietary patients achieved a six-point reduction in Reflux Symptom Index versus 54.1% on PPIs. Separately, a non-inferiority randomised controlled trial found magnesium alginate non-inferior to proton pump inhibitors for laryngopharyngeal reflux.
impact: Undermines empiric high-dose PPI as the default first move in laryngopharyngeal reflux, where the mechanism is often non-acid or mixed and acid suppression is treating the wrong thing.
practical: Start with diet, reflux precautions and an alginate rather than a PPI, and reserve acid suppression for demonstrated acid reflux. The alginate trial is the stronger citation of the two — it is a randomised non-inferiority design, whereas the dietary comparison is a retrospective single-centre study from 2017 with a symptom-index endpoint and no objective reflux testing.
link: JAMA Otolaryngology — alkaline water and Mediterranean diet versus proton pump inhibition for laryngopharyngeal reflux

verify.note: The study is real and the journal is right, but not the year or the design. Zalvan et al., JAMA Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery 2017;143(10):1023-1029: alkaline water plus a plant-based Mediterranean-style diet plus reflux precautions versus PPI plus precautions, with 62.6% versus 54.1% achieving a six-point Reflux Symptom Index reduction. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) Date and scope: submitted as 'multi-center comparisons in JAMA Otolaryngology' in 2026; it is a single 2017 study, retrospective, with a symptom-index endpoint and no objective reflux testing. (2) The submission recommends alginates without citing anything for them — a magnesium alginate versus PPI non-inferiority randomised controlled trial exists and has been added, because it is the better-designed of the two studies and is the actual evidence behind the recommendation the submission makes. The clinical direction — do not escalate empiric PPIs for non-acid or mixed reflux without objective testing — is sound and is kept.

title: Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation and Downstream Metabolic and Cardiovascular Outcomes
journal: Registry analyses and the CARDIOSA-12 randomised trial
breakthrough: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation in obstructive sleep apnea has been associated with a lower two-year incidence of newly diagnosed diabetes and hypertension compared with PAP-intolerant patients who did not receive it. The signal is time-dependent: an increased rate of hypertension diagnosis was observed within the first two years, with reduced risk emerging after two years. CARDIOSA-12, a randomised sham-controlled double-blind crossover trial at the University of Pennsylvania, examined cardiovascular endpoints directly.
impact: Extends the case for treating OSA surgically beyond symptom relief towards metabolic and vascular risk — but as a hypothesis-generating signal, not a demonstrated outcome.
practical: Do not counsel a patient that hypoglossal nerve stimulation will prevent stroke: stroke reduction has not been shown, and the follow-up in these analyses is too short to see arrhythmia, coronary disease or heart failure. The defensible statement is that two-year new diagnoses of diabetes and hypertension were lower in treated patients than in PAP-intolerant controls, in observational comparisons where the treated group differs from the untreated in ways adjustment cannot fully handle.
link: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation and cardiovascular outcomes in obstructive sleep apnea

verify.status: corrected — one claimed outcome not shown, and the signal is not one-directional
verify.note: Partly supported, with two corrections that change the counselling. (1) STROKE NOT SHOWN. The submission claims registry studies evaluated 'reduction in hypertension and stroke incidence'. What is reported is a lower two-year incidence of new diabetes and hypertension versus PAP-intolerant patients; stroke reduction was not demonstrated, and the follow-up is explicitly described as too short to observe arrhythmias, coronary artery disease or heart failure. (2) The hypertension finding is time-dependent — an INCREASED risk of hypertension diagnosis within the first two years, with reduced risk after two years — which the submission's one-directional framing hides. The conclusion that this 'elevates sleep surgery from a purely symptomatic quality-of-life intervention to a validated cardiorespiratory risk-reduction therapy' is therefore not supported; 'validated' is wrong for an observational signal with a confounded comparison group. CARDIOSA-12 (NCT03359096), a randomised sham-controlled crossover trial of cardiovascular endpoints, is cited as the design capable of answering the question.

title: Image Guidance, Augmented Reality and Robotics in Endoscopic Skull Base Surgery
breakthrough: Image-guided navigation is now routine in endoscopic skull base surgery for identifying critical anatomy. Augmented reality and 3D visualisation have been associated with a fall in internal carotid artery injury rates from 0.9% to 0.3%. Robotic assistance combined with opto-electrical navigation has been reported with a mean navigated accuracy of 1.53 mm, and robotic technology is being applied in lateral skull base work for acoustic neuroma and cholesteatoma where the facial nerve and cochlear apparatus must be preserved.
impact: The carotid injury figure is the concrete gain: a threefold reduction in the complication that kills people in this operation, attributed to better intraoperative visualisation rather than to a new technique.
practical: Navigation and augmented reality are worth the setup time in revision and extended approaches, where the landmarks that normally protect the carotid are gone. Keep expectations of the robotics realistic — 1.53 mm navigated accuracy is a bench-and-series figure, not a clinical outcome, and no study has demonstrated that robotic assistance shortens operating time or reduces cranial nerve injury. Verify anatomy against the endoscopic view, not the overlay.
link: Robotic-assisted surgery in skull-base procedures: advances, applications and emerging innovations

verify.status: corrected — real technology, the claimed outcomes are not established
verify.note: The technology is real: image-guided navigation is standard, augmented reality and 3D visualisation are associated with internal carotid artery injury falling from 0.9% to 0.3%, a robotic-plus-navigation system has been reported at 1.53 mm mean navigated accuracy, and robotics is used in lateral skull base surgery around the facial nerve. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) The submission says this 'sets new surgical safety standards for image-guided endoscopic transsphenoidal and temporal bone procedures'. No standard has been set — these are series and reviews, not a standards document. (2) 'Enhances surgical precision, reduces operative times, and lowers rates of iatrogenic cranial nerve injury' — none of the operative-time or cranial-nerve-injury claims is established, and the entry now says so explicitly. The carotid injury figure was missing from the submission and has been added as the one hard number available; it is also the point most worth teaching, since it attaches the benefit to visualisation in revision anatomy rather than to robotics in general.
